Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   I.       INTRODUCTION
                                  14            In this action, Plaintiff Extend, Inc. (“Extend”) seeks to recover payments Defendant

                                  15   MyPillow, Inc. (“MyPillow”) promised to make under a March 2024 Termination Agreement

                                  16   (“Termination Agreement”). Extend filed its complaint on August 30, 2024 asserting a single

                                  17   claim for breach of contract. MyPillow failed to appear or answer the complaint and the Clerk

                                  18   entered default against it on October 28, 2024. Dkt. No. 13. Presently before the Court is

                                  19   Extend’s Motion for Default Judgment (“Motion”). Because MyPillow has not appeared or

                                  20   consented to the jurisdiction of the undersigned magistrate judge pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 636(c),

                                  21   the case shall be reassigned to a district court judge for disposition with the following Report and

                                  22   Recommendation. On December 18, 2024, a hearing was held on the Motion, and thereafter

                                  23   Extend submitted supplemental materials in support of the Motion. For the reasons stated below,

                                  24   the Court RECOMMENDS that the Motion be GRANTED.

                                  25   II.      BACKGROUND
                                  26            A.        The Complaint
                                  27            Extend is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in San Francisco,

                                  28   California. Compl. ¶ 1. MyPillow is a Minnesota corporation based in Chaska, Minnesota. Id. ¶
                                         Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL              Document 21         Filed 01/16/25      Page 2 of 8




                                   1   2. In November 2022, Extend entered into a contract with MyPillow to provide MyPillow’s

                                   2   customers with shipping and product protection services in exchange for a percentage of revenues

                                   3   generated by the sale of those services (the “Agreement”). Id. ¶ 9. In March 2024, MyPillow was

                                   4   overdue on its payments under the Agreement. Id. ¶ 10; see also Compl., Ex. A (Termination

                                   5   Agreement), Preamble (stating that “MyPillow owe[d] Extend a total of $453,352.17 as of the end

                                   6   of February 2024).

                                   7           On March 29, 2024, the parties entered into the Termination Agreement, which terminated

                                   8   the Agreement effective April 1, 2024 and obligated MyPillow to make the following payments:

                                   9               •     April 3, 2024: $75,000

                                  10               •     April 17, 2024: $100,000

                                  11               •     May 8, 2024: $100,000

                                  12               •     May 29, 2024: $125,000
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13               •      June 12, 2024: $53,352.17

                                  14               •     “any additional amount due and owing under the Agreement related to the sale of

                                  15                     Extend services during the month of March 2024.”

                                  16   Compl., Ex. A (Termination Agreement), Sections 1, 3. The Termination Agreement contained

                                  17   the following forum selection and choice of law provision:

                                  18                     Governing Law; Choice of Forum. This Agreement will be
                                                         governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State
                                  19                     of California, without giving effect to any principles of conflict of
                                                         laws. Any legal action or proceeding arising under this Agreement
                                  20                     will be brought exclusively in the federal or state courts located in San
                                                         Francisco, California and the parties hereto irrevocably consent to
                                  21                     personal jurisdiction and venue therein.

                                  22   Id., Section 5.

                                  23           MyPillow owed Extend $110,799.22 under the Agreement for Extend’s services during

                                  24   March 2024. Compl. ¶ 11. On April 4, 2024, Extend emailed an invoice to MyPillow for these

                                  25   services, including a spreadsheet reflecting the transactions upon which the amount due for March

                                  26   2024 was based. Id. ¶ 12 & Ex. B (invoice); see also dkt. no. 20 (Second Supplemental

                                  27   Declaration of Ethan Jacobs in Support of Motion for Default Judgment) (summarizing contents of

                                  28   spreadsheet an attesting to total amount of $110,799.22).
                                                                                            2
                                          Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL         Document 21         Filed 01/16/25     Page 3 of 8




                                   1          In May 2024, MyPillow did not make any payments under the Termination Agreement and

                                   2   Extend’s counsel sent MyPillow a demand for payment. Compl. ¶ 12. On June 23, 2024, Mike

                                   3   Lindell, Chief Executive Officer of MyPillow, emailed that he would ‘connect this week[ ]’ [b]ut

                                   4   Mr. Lindell did not connect, and never did.” Id. ¶ 14. Since June 2024, MyPillow “has ignored

                                   5   repeated inquiries and demand for payment . . . and has not paid any of the amounts due under the

                                   6   Termination Agreement.” Id. ¶ 15.

                                   7          Extend initiated this action on August 30, 2024. In its breach of contract complaint, it

                                   8   seeks compensatory damages, costs of suit and pre- and post-judgment interest. Compl. at p. 4.

                                   9          B.    The Motion
                                  10          In the Motion, Extend asks the Court to enter default judgment against MyPillow and

                                  11   award $564,151.39 in compensatory damages. According to Extend, the amount of damages it

                                  12   seeks is “exactly the amount set out as MyPillow’s payment obligation under the Termination
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Agreement: $453,352.17 in payments specified in Section 3, and $110,799.22 for the “additional

                                  14   amount due and owing … related to the sale of Extend services during the Month of March 2024”

                                  15   and reflected in the invoice attached as Exhibit B to the Complaint.” Motion at 5.

                                  16   III.   ANALYSIS
                                  17          A.    Legal Standards Governing Entry of Default Judgment
                                  18          Pursuant to Rule 55(b)(2) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, a court may enter a

                                  19   default judgment where the clerk, under Rule 55(a), has previously entered the party’s default

                                  20   based upon failure to plead or otherwise defend the action. Fed. R. Civ. P. 55(b). The Court may

                                  21   not enter default judgment against a minor or incompetent person unless he or she is adequately

                                  22   represented. Id. A plaintiff seeking default judgment also must aver that the defendant is not in

                                  23   military service entitled to the benefits of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act of 2003. See 50

                                  24   App. U.S.C.A. § 521(b)(1). Once a party’s default has been entered, the factual allegations of the

                                  25   complaint, except those concerning damages, are deemed true. Fed. R. Civ. Proc. 8(b)(6).

                                  26          A defendant’s default, however, does not automatically entitle the plaintiff to a court-

                                  27   ordered default judgment. Draper v. Coombs, 792 F.2d 915, 924-25 (9th Cir. 1986). “The district

                                  28   court’s decision whether to enter a default judgment is a discretionary one.” Aldabe v. Aldabe,
                                                                                        3
                                            Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL        Document 21        Filed 01/16/25      Page 4 of 8




                                   1   616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980). If the court is satisfied that jurisdiction is proper and that

                                   2   service of process upon the defendant was adequate, courts are instructed to consider several facts

                                   3   in determining whether to grant default judgment:

                                   4                  (1) the possibility of prejudice to the plaintiff, (2) the merits of
                                                      plaintiff’s substantive claim, (3) the sufficiency of the complaint, (4)
                                   5                  the sum of money at stake in the action, (5) the possibility of a
                                                      dispute concerning material facts, (6) whether the default was due to
                                   6                  excusable neglect, and (7) the strong policy underlying the Federal
                                                      Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on the merits.
                                   7

                                   8   Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471-72 (9th Cir. 1986). In reviewing the plaintiff’s substantive

                                   9   claims and the sufficiency of the complaint, the factual allegations, except those concerning

                                  10   damages, are deemed to have been admitted by the non-responding party. TeleVideo Systems, Inc.

                                  11   v. Heidenthal, 826 F.2d 915, 917-18 (9th Cir. 1987) (citing Geddes v. United Fin. Grp., 559 F.2d

                                  12   557, 560 (9th Cir. 1977)).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           B.   Adequacy of Service
                                  14           As a preliminary matter, where entry of default judgment is requested, the Court must

                                  15   determine whether service of process was adequate. Bank of the West v. RMA Lumber Inc., No. C

                                  16   07-06469 JSW, 2008 WL 2474650, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 17, 2008). The Court concludes that

                                  17   service was proper.

                                  18           Plaintiff has supplied a proof of service showing that the complaint and summons were

                                  19   personally served on Doug Wardlow, who is general counsel for MyPillow, at 1550 Audubon Rd,

                                  20   Chaska, MN 55318. Dkt. no. 11. According to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s business search

                                  21   website, of which the Court takes judicial notice, the address where Wardlow was served is the

                                  22   MyPillow corporate offices address. See https://mblsportal.sos.state.mn.us/Business/

                                  23   SearchDetails?filingGuid=52337245-94d4-e011-a886-001ec94ffe7f. “While the Ninth Circuit has

                                  24   not addressed this issue, other courts have held that service on the general counsel of a corporation

                                  25   constitutes service on a “managing or general agent” under Rule 4(h)(1)(B).”1 Boards of Trustees

                                  26
                                  27
                                       1
                                         Rule 4(h)(1)(B) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure provides for service on a corporation “in
                                       a judicial district of the United States” “by delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint
                                  28   to an officer, a managing or general agent, or any other agent authorized by appointment or by law
                                       to receive service of process . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(h)(1)(B).
                                                                                           4
                                         Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL              Document 21           Filed 01/16/25   Page 5 of 8




                                   1   of AGC Operating Eng'r Health & Welfare Fund v. Ross Island Sand & Gravel Co, No. 3:19-CV-

                                   2   02025-YY, 2020 WL 5507276, at *2 (D. Or. May 27, 2020), report and recommendation adopted

                                   3   in part sub nom. Boards of Trustees of Agc-Operating Eng'r Health & Welfare Fund v. Ross

                                   4   Island Sand & Gravel Co., No. 3:19-CV-2025-YY, 2020 WL 3265394 (D. Or. June 17, 2020)

                                   5   (citing United States v. Cornwell, No. 6:18-cv-2194-Orl-22EJK, 2020 WL 674092, at *5 (M.D.

                                   6   Fla. Feb. 11, 2020); American Centennial Ins. Co. v. Handal, 901 F. Supp. 892 899 (D.N.J.

                                   7   1995)).

                                   8             Here, the Court finds that service on MyPillow’s general counsel at its corporate office

                                   9   constituted sufficient service on a “managing or general agent” for purposes of satisfying Rule

                                  10   4(h)(1)(B).

                                  11          C.      Jurisdiction
                                  12             Extend has alleged sufficient facts to establish that there is subject matter jurisdiction
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   based on diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1132 because the parties are citizens of different states and

                                  14   more than $75,000 is in controversy. Further, MyPillow has consented to this Court’s personal

                                  15   jurisdiction under the Termination Agreement by agreeing to the forum selection clause in that

                                  16   agreement. See Homelink Int’l Inc. v. Zhang, No. 24-CV-02358-VKD, 2024 WL 4197634, at *7

                                  17   (N.D. Cal. Sept. 12, 2024) (“Under federal law, a valid forum selection clause operates as consent

                                  18   to a court’s personal jurisdiction.”) (citing Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 473

                                  19   n.14 (1985) (recognizing that personal jurisdiction is “waivable” through “a variety of legal

                                  20   arrangements,” including forum selection provisions)). Accordingly, the Court has jurisdiction

                                  21   over this action.

                                  22          D.      Eitel Factors
                                  23                   1. Possibility of Prejudice to Plaintiff
                                  24             The first factor established by the Ninth Circuit in Eitel considers whether the plaintiff

                                  25   would be prejudiced by denial of default judgment. Craigslist, Inc. v. Naturemarket, Inc., 694 F.

                                  26   Supp. 2d 1039, 1054 (N.D. Cal. 2010). Extend will be prejudiced by denial of default judgment

                                  27   because if this Court denies its request for default judgment, Extend will be left without a remedy.

                                  28   See PepsiCo, Inc. v. California Sec. Cans, 238 F. Supp. 2d 1172, 1177 (C.D. Cal. 2002).
                                                                                            5
                                         Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL            Document 21         Filed 01/16/25      Page 6 of 8




                                   1   Accordingly, this factor weighs in favor of entry of default judgment.

                                   2                2. Merits of plaintiff’s claim and sufficiency of complaint
                                   3          Next, the Court must consider the sufficiency of the allegations and the substantive merits

                                   4   of Extend’s breach of contract claim to determine whether entry of default judgment is warranted.

                                   5   Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471. In California, the elements of a cause of action for breach of contract are:

                                   6   1) the existence of the contract; 2) performance by the plaintiff or excuse for nonperformance; 3)

                                   7   breach by the defendant; and 4) resulting damages to the plaintiff. Oasis W. Realty, LLC v.

                                   8   Goldman, 51 Cal. 4th 811, 821 (2011) (citing Reichert v. Gen. Ins. Co. of Am., 68 Cal. 2d 822, 830

                                   9   (1968)). Plaintiff’s breach of contract claim is sufficient, both as a matter of pleading and on the

                                  10   merits. Plaintiff has alleged the existence of the Termination Agreement, that it “did all the

                                  11   significant things that the Termination Agreement required it to do[,]” that MyPillow failed to

                                  12   make the payments it agreed to under the Termination Agreement, and that Extend has been
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   damaged as a result. Compl. ¶¶ 16-20. In addition, Extend supplied a copy of the Termination

                                  14   Agreement as an attachment to the Complaint. Therefore, this factor weighs in favor of entry of

                                  15   default judgment.

                                  16                3. Amount of money at stake
                                  17          The court must also consider the amount a plaintiff requests in monetary damages. Elektra

                                  18   Ent. Grp. Inc. v. Crawford, 226 F.R.D. 388, 393 (C.D. Cal. 2005) (citing Eitel, 782 F.2d at

                                  19   1471−72). Here, Extend requests damages of $564,151.39. This sum is “significant” but it is

                                  20   reasonable because it is “the amount indicated by the [agreement’s] own terms.” Williams v. La

                                  21   Perla N. Am., Inc., No. 3:23-CV-01633-JSC, 2024 WL 1974546, at *4 (N.D. Cal. May 3, 2024)

                                  22   (finding a default judgment of $1,362,506.82 based on past rent owed was reasonable because it

                                  23   was supported by the lease terms). Therefore, this factor supports entry of default judgment.

                                  24                4. Possibility of disputed material facts
                                  25          The fifth Eitel factor weighs the possibility that material facts may be in dispute. Eitel,

                                  26   782 F.2d at 1471-72. In light of the clear terms of the Termination Agreement and the allegations

                                  27   in the Complaint, the Court finds that there is not a significant possibility that there are disputes of

                                  28   material fact. Therefore, this factor weighs in favor of entry of default judgment.
                                                                                          6
                                         Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL           Document 21         Filed 01/16/25    Page 7 of 8




                                   1                5. Excusable neglect

                                   2          Under the sixth Eitel factor, courts consider whether the defendant’s default may have been

                                   3   the product of excusable neglect. Id. Here, MyPillow was properly served and there is no

                                   4   indication that its default was due to excusable neglect. Indeed, Extend has supplied a declaration

                                   5   of counsel indicating that MyPillow’s general counsel exchanged email communications with him

                                   6   after the lawsuit was served, indicating that MyPillow was aware of the lawsuit but failed to

                                   7   respond. See Declaration of Ethan Jacobs, dkt. no. 14-1, ¶ 5 (“After Extend served MyPillow

                                   8   through Mr. Wardlow, he and I exchanged several emails regarding the possibility of MyPillow

                                   9   negotiating a settlement agreement to resolve this lawsuit, and the last email I received from him

                                  10   was on October 16, 2024.”). This factor therefore favors entry of default judgment.

                                  11                6. Policy in favor of judgment on the merits
                                  12          Finally, the seventh Eitel factor considers the policy that generally disfavors default
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   judgments because “cases should be decided upon their merits whenever reasonably possible.” Id.

                                  14   at 1472. However, a resolution of the dispute on the merits it not possible because MyPillow has

                                  15   failed to appear. Therefore, this factor favors entry of default judgment.

                                  16                7. Conclusion
                                  17          Based on its consideration of the Eitel factors, the undersigned recommends that default

                                  18   judgment be entered against MyPillow.

                                  19          E.    Damages
                                  20          Having determined that entry of default judgment is warranted, the Court now must

                                  21   determine the appropriate remedy. See Geddes v. United Fin. Group, 559 F.2d 557, 560 (9th Cir.

                                  22   1977). Under Rule 54(c), the scope of relief “must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount,

                                  23   what is demanded in the pleadings.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(c). Further, a plaintiff seeking default

                                  24   judgment “must ‘prove up’ the amount of damages that it is claiming.” Philip Morris USA, Inc. v.

                                  25   Castworld Products,Inc., 219 F.R.D. 494, 501 (C.D. Cal. 2003).

                                  26          Extend seeks compensatory damages in the amount of $564,151.39, that is, the

                                  27   $453,352.17 in payments that are listed in the Termination Agreement and the $110,799.22

                                  28   payment for March 2024, which is specifically provided for under the Termination Agreement and
                                                                                         7
                                         Case 3:24-cv-06152-RFL          Document 21         Filed 01/16/25    Page 8 of 8




                                   1   reflected in the invoice attached to the complaint. These damages are adequately supported and

                                   2   should be awarded in full.

                                   3   IV.    CONCLUSION
                                   4          For the reasons stated above, the undersigned recommends that the Court GRANT the

                                   5   Motion, enter default judgment against MyPillow and award $564,151.39 in damages. Extend is

                                   6   ordered to serve a copy of this Report on MyPillow and file a proof of service to that effect. Any

                                   7   party may file objections to the recommendations in this Report within fourteen days of being

                                   8   served with a copy. See 28 U.S.C. § 636(b).

                                   9          IT IS SO ORDERED.
